glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Jesus, a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, holds a priesthood greater than Levi’s because God swore it by oath, it rests on His endless life, and He offered Himself once for all, so He is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through Him.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Hebrews 7 resumes the subject announced in 5:10 and 6:20. It draws on Genesis 14:18–20, where Melchizedek, king of Salem, blessed Abraham, and on God’s oath in Psalm 110:4.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Therefore He is also able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through Him, since He always lives to make intercession for them.” (Hebrews 7:25)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Hebrews returns to a figure who appears only briefly in Genesis. Melchizedek, “king of Salem, priest of the Most High God,” met Abraham after a battle, blessed him, and received a tenth of the spoils (7:1–2). His name means “king of righteousness,” and Salem means peace. Genesis records no parents, genealogy, birth, or death for him, and Hebrews uses that silence to present him as “made like the Son of God” (7:3). He was a real, historical king and priest who foreshadowed Christ. The greatness of his priesthood shows in Abraham’s actions. The father of Israel gave him a tenth and received his blessing, and “beyond all contradiction the lesser is blessed by the better” (7:7). In a sense, even Levi paid tithes through Abraham.

Then Hebrews draws the conclusion. If the Levitical priesthood could have made people perfect, God would not have promised another priest. Jesus came from Judah, not Levi, so a new priesthood means a new order. His priesthood rests “according to the power of an endless life” (7:16), and God confirmed it with an oath: “The LORD has sworn And will not relent” (7:21). That makes Jesus “a surety of a better covenant” (7:22), its personal guarantor.

The chapter’s climax is personal. Israel’s priests died and had to be replaced, but Jesus “continues forever” (7:24). “Therefore He is also able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through Him, since He always lives to make intercession for them” (7:25). He is holy and without sin, so He never needed to offer for Himself, and He offered Himself “once for all” (7:27).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Hebrews 7:1–3 — Melchizedek, King and Priest

Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, blessed Abraham and received a tenth of the spoils. His name means king of righteousness, Salem means peace, and because Genesis records no beginning or end for him, he is made like the Son of God as a picture of an unending priesthood.

Hebrews 7:4–10 — Greater Than Abraham and Levi

Abraham’s gift of a tenth and Melchizedek’s blessing show Melchizedek’s greater standing, for the lesser is blessed by the greater. The Levitical priests were mortal men who received tithes, and in a sense Levi himself paid tithes to Melchizedek through his ancestor Abraham.

Hebrews 7:11–19 — A New Priest and a Change of Law

God’s promise of a priest like Melchizedek shows that the Levitical priesthood could not make anyone perfect, and a change of priesthood requires a change of law. Jesus came from Judah, not Levi, and He is priest by the power of an endless life, bringing a better hope through which we draw near to God.

Hebrews 7:20–22 — The Oath and the Better Covenant

Israel’s priests took office without an oath, but God appointed Jesus with a sworn promise that He will not take back. That makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.

Hebrews 7:23–25 — He Always Lives to Intercede

Death kept Israel’s priests from continuing in office, but Jesus lives forever and holds His priesthood permanently. He is therefore able to save completely those who come to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them.

Hebrews 7:26–28 — The Holy High Priest Who Offered Himself Once

Jesus is the holy, sinless, exalted High Priest that sinners need. He has no need to offer sacrifices for His own sins, and He offered Himself once for all, appointed by God’s oath as the Son who has completed His calling forever.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Hebrews 7 shows why believers can draw near to God with confidence. Their High Priest will never die, never be replaced, and never stop interceding for them. His salvation is complete and lasting because He Himself lives forever and stands before God on their behalf (7:24–25).

The chapter also shows that God planned this change long before it came. Psalm 110, written while the Levitical priesthood still served, already promised a priest of a different order. The law and its priests were God’s good gifts, but they could not bring people fully near to Him, and Jesus brings the better hope they pointed toward (7:11, 19).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Melchizedek and the Son. A historical king-priest made like the Son of God foreshadows Jesus’ priesthood (7:1–3).

Greater than Levi. Abraham’s tenth and Melchizedek’s blessing show the greater priesthood (7:4–10).

A better hope. The law made nothing perfect, but Jesus brings a hope by which we draw near to God (7:11–19).

God’s oath. God swore that Jesus is a priest forever, making Him the guarantor of a better covenant (7:20–22).

He always lives to intercede. Jesus’ endless life and once-for-all offering make His salvation complete (7:23–28).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Melchizedek (7:1). The king of Salem, ancient Jerusalem, and priest of God Most High who blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18–20). He was a real person and a type of Christ. Hebrews says he was “made like the Son of God,” not that he was the Son.

Without father, without mother (7:3). Genesis records no family line, birth, or death for Melchizedek. Hebrews uses that silence to picture a priesthood without end.

A tenth (7:2, 4). Abraham’s gift of a tenth of the spoils shows Melchizedek’s greater standing, which is the point of the argument here. The tenth also appears before the law (Genesis 28:22), under the law (Leviticus 27:30), and in Jesus’ teaching (Matthew 23:23), and this passage supports the biblical practice of tithing. The New Testament gives no direct command to tithe, and Christians differ on how it applies today.

The Levitical priesthood (7:11). The priests descended from Levi and Aaron who served under the law of Moses.

Surety (7:22). A guarantor who stands behind a pledge. Jesus Himself guarantees the better covenant.

To the uttermost (7:25). Completely and forever. Jesus’ salvation lacks nothing and never runs out, because He always lives to intercede.

focus: Hebrews 7 explains why Jesus, a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, holds a priesthood greater than that of the Levitical priests, arguing from Melchizedek’s standing over Abraham, the change of law a new priest requires, God’s oath, and the Son’s endless life. Because He continues forever, holy and without sin, having offered Himself once for all, Jesus is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through Him.

sections.title: Melchizedek, King and Priest
sections.summary: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, blessed him, and received a tenth of all. His name and title mean king of righteousness and king of peace, and Scripture records no father, mother, genealogy, beginning, or end for him, so that he is “made like the Son of God” (Hebrews 7:3) and remains a priest continually.

sections.title: Greater Than Abraham and Levi
sections.summary: “Now consider how great this man was” (Hebrews 7:4): the patriarch Abraham gave him a tenth of the spoils, and beyond all contradiction the lesser is blessed by the better. The Levitical priests receive tithes as mortal men, yet Levi himself, so to speak, paid tithes through Abraham to one of whom it is witnessed that he lives.

sections.title: A New Priest and a Change of Law
sections.summary: If perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood, there would have been no need for another priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and a change of priesthood requires a change of law. Jesus arose from Judah, a tribe Moses never connected with priesthood, and He became priest “according to the power of an endless life” (Hebrews 7:16), so the weak former commandment is annulled and a better hope is brought in, through which we draw near to God.

sections.title: The Oath and the Better Covenant
sections.summary: The Levitical priests became priests without an oath, but Jesus was appointed by God’s sworn word: “The LORD has sworn And will not relent” (Hebrews 7:21). By so much more Jesus has become “a surety of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22), that is, its personal guarantor.

sections.title: He Always Lives to Intercede
sections.summary: The former priests were many, because death prevented them from continuing, but Jesus continues forever and holds an unchangeable priesthood. “Therefore He is also able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through Him, since He always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

sections.title: The Holy High Priest Who Offered Himself Once
sections.summary: Such a High Priest was fitting for us: holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and higher than the heavens. Unlike the high priests who offer daily for their own sins and then for the people’s, He offered up Himself once for all, and the word of the oath appoints “the Son who has been perfected forever” (Hebrews 7:28).

1.brief: Hebrews returns to Melchizedek, “king of Salem, priest of the Most High God,” who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him. Drawing on Genesis 14, the writer presents a real, historical king and priest who ruled Salem, ancient Jerusalem.
1.explain: “king of Salem, priest of the Most High God” Genesis 14:18–20 presents Melchizedek as a historical king and priest. He met Abraham after the defeat of the kings who had taken Lot and blessed him. Salem is associated with Jerusalem in Psalm 76:2. The two offices in one man prepare for Hebrews’ comparison to the royal priest promised in Psalm 110.

2.brief: Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything, honoring his standing, and his name and title mean “king of righteousness” and “king of peace.” Hebrews draws attention to the meaning of his name and title, since righteousness and peace belong to this king-priest.
2.explain: “Abraham gave a tenth part of all” Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils of the victory, acknowledging his priestly standing. The name Melchizedek is interpreted as king of righteousness, and Salem supplies the title king of peace. Hebrews foregrounds both titles in its portrait of this king-priest.

3.brief: Genesis records no father, mother, genealogy, birth, or death for Melchizedek, and in this way he is “made like the Son of God” and “remains a priest continually.” Hebrews uses what Scripture leaves unrecorded to make this historical king-priest a likeness of the Son’s unending priesthood.
3.explain: “made like the Son of God” Genesis names no parents, pedigree, birth, or death for Melchizedek. The account leaves him standing as priest without recording who preceded or succeeded him. Hebrews uses the way Genesis presents this real man as a type of the Son’s enduring priesthood. Melchizedek is made like the Son, and the Son’s own endless life is what makes His priesthood permanent.

4.brief: “Now consider how great this man was, to whom even the patriarch Abraham gave a tenth of the spoils.” By giving him the tenth, Abraham, the honored father of Israel, acknowledged Melchizedek’s greater standing, and he did so long before the law of Moses.
4.explain: “even the patriarch Abraham gave a tenth of the spoils” The writer appeals to the greatness of Abraham in Israel’s story so the gift will carry its full weight. If the patriarch honored Melchizedek this way, Melchizedek’s priestly standing must be taken seriously. Abraham’s tenth also precedes the law. The practice appears again before Sinai, is confirmed under the law, and is affirmed by Jesus in His words to the scribes and Pharisees (Genesis 28:22, Leviticus 27:30, and Matthew 23:23). Christians differ on its continuing force, and the New Testament gives the church no direct command to tithe.

5.brief: The descendants of Levi who become priests are commanded by the law to receive tithes from the people, their own brothers, even though all of them descended from Abraham. The Levitical priests received tithes by legal right from people of the same family.
5.explain: “have a commandment to receive tithes” The sons of Levi who hold priestly office receive tithes under the law from other descendants of Abraham. The priests and those who give are therefore relatives by descent. This legal right sets up the striking case of a priest who receives a tenth from Abraham himself.

6.brief: Melchizedek, whose genealogy does not come from Levi, received tithes from Abraham and blessed the man “who had the promises.” Though his priesthood did not come through Levi’s line, he stood above Abraham in this meeting, receiving Abraham’s tenth and giving him a blessing.
6.explain: “he whose genealogy is not derived from them” Melchizedek has no place in Levi’s priestly line. Yet he receives a tenth from Abraham and blesses the man who possesses God’s promises. The fact that Abraham is already the recipient of the promises gives the blessing particular weight.

7.brief: “Now beyond all contradiction the lesser is blessed by the better.” By blessing Abraham, Melchizedek showed that he held the greater position.
7.explain: “the lesser is blessed by the better” In this solemn blessing the person who confers it stands above the person who receives it. The comparison concerns priestly standing. Abraham’s importance is precisely what makes the incident significant.

8.brief: Under the law, mortal men receive tithes, but in Melchizedek’s case the tithe was received by one “of whom it is witnessed that he lives.” Scripture’s silence about his death makes him a picture of a priesthood that does not end.
8.explain: “Here mortal men receive tithes” The Levitical recipients die, as the writer will stress again in verse 23. In Genesis, the testimony about Melchizedek leaves him on the page in the role of a living priest, with no death reported. That contrast serves the comparison with Christ, who actually lives forever.

9.brief: Even Levi, who receives tithes, “paid tithes through Abraham, so to speak.” The tribe of priests, in a sense, honored Melchizedek through its forefather.
9.explain: “paid tithes through Abraham, so to speak” Levi ordinarily stands on the receiving side of the tithe. In Abraham’s representative act Hebrews can speak of Levi as giving a tenth to Melchizedek. The words “so to speak” mark the indirect character of the argument.

10.brief: Levi was still “in the loins of his father” when Melchizedek met Abraham, which is the writer’s way of saying that Levi was a future descendant of Abraham, not yet born. The words “so to speak” in Hebrews 7:9 mark this as a figure: Abraham’s act represented his descendants, so the Levitical priesthood stands beneath Melchizedek’s.
10.explain: “he was still in the loins of his father” Levi was a future descendant of Abraham when Melchizedek met the patriarch. What Abraham did therefore matters to the comparison with the priestly tribe that later came from him.

11.brief: If perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood, under which the people received the law, there would be no need for another priest to arise “according to the order of Melchizedek, and not be called according to the order of Aaron.” God’s promise of a different priest shows that the Levitical priesthood could not bring people fully to God.
11.explain: “if perfection were through the Levitical priesthood” Perfection here means reaching the intended goal of bringing worshipers fully to God. Israel received the law in connection with the Levitical priesthood. Yet the later promise of another priest in Melchizedek’s order raises the decisive question: why would God give another priest if Aaron’s order had already brought worshipers to that goal?

12.brief: “For the priesthood being changed, of necessity there is also a change of the law.” The law was bound up with the Levitical priesthood, so a new priesthood requires a new legal order.
12.explain: “a change of the law” The law specifies who may serve under the earlier order. A different priesthood necessarily means a change in the law governing it. The examples that follow begin with eligibility and lead toward the better covenant in Hebrews 7:22 and 8:6.

13.brief: Jesus, of whom these things are spoken, belongs to another tribe, from which no man has ever served at the altar. The promised priest does not come from Levi at all.
13.explain: “belongs to another tribe” The One addressed in Psalm 110 belongs to a tribe that supplied no priest to serve at the altar under Moses. His priesthood therefore calls for an appointment other than Aaronic descent.

14.brief: Scripture makes it evident that our Lord arose from Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priesthood. Jesus’ descent from Judah shows that His priesthood rests on a different basis than the law of Moses.
14.explain: “our Lord arose from Judah” Jesus belongs to Judah. Moses gives Judah no priestly role. The difference in tribe makes plain why the law that governed priestly descent cannot account for Jesus’ office.

15.brief: The point becomes even clearer since another priest arises “in the likeness of Melchizedek.” Jesus’ priesthood follows the pattern of Melchizedek rather than the pattern of Aaron.
15.explain: “in the likeness of Melchizedek” The kind of priest God promised makes the change clearer still. Jesus belongs to the pattern of Melchizedek, and the next verse identifies the basis on which He holds the office.

16.brief: The new priest has come “not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an endless life.” His priesthood rests not on physical descent but on the life He has as the risen One, a life that cannot end.
16.explain: “the power of an endless life” A command tied to physical descent governed the earlier priesthood. Jesus’ enduring life, displayed in His resurrection, is the ground of His permanent office. His life gives content to the word forever in God’s promise.

17.brief: God testifies of Him in Psalm 110, “You are a priest forever According to the order of Melchizedek.” The word forever confirms that His priesthood is founded on endless life.
17.explain: “You are a priest forever” God’s testimony from Psalm 110:4 confirms that Jesus occupies this office permanently. The words also give the divine warrant for His priesthood in a different order.

18.brief: There is an annulling of the former commandment about the priesthood “because of its weakness and unprofitableness.” The old priestly order is set aside because it could not make worshipers perfect or bring them fully near to God.
18.explain: “an annulling of the former commandment” The earlier priestly command is set aside because it cannot do what Hebrews is asking of a priesthood. Its weakness is measured against the goal of bringing worshipers all the way into God’s presence.

19.brief: “For the law made nothing perfect,” but a better hope has been brought in, “through which we draw near to God.” What the law could not do, the better hope in Christ does: it brings people near to God.
19.explain: “through which we draw near to God” The law could bring no worshiper to the completion at issue. The better hope gives actual access to God through the living Priest. Drawing near is the practical result the whole comparison has been moving toward.

20.brief: Jesus was not made a priest without an oath. God’s sworn word sets His priesthood apart from all others.
20.explain: “He was not made priest without an oath” Hebrews introduces an additional ground for confidence in Jesus’ priesthood. God appointed Him with an oath, and that sworn appointment leads to the conclusion about the better covenant in verse 22.

21.brief: The Levitical priests became priests without an oath, but Jesus became priest with an oath from God: “The LORD has sworn And will not relent, ‘You are a priest forever According to the order of Melchizedek.’” God’s oath makes Jesus’ priesthood permanent and unchangeable.
21.explain: “The LORD has sworn And will not relent” The earlier priests received their office under the law. The Son received this sworn word from God, who will never withdraw it. The oath confirms the forever of His appointment.

22.brief: By so much more Jesus has become “a surety of a better covenant,” its personal guarantor. God’s oath established Jesus as a priest forever, and as that priest Jesus Himself guarantees the better covenant He brings.
22.explain: “a surety of a better covenant” A surety is a person who guarantees what has been pledged. Jesus Himself, appointed by God’s oath and living forever, guarantees the better covenant. Chapter 8 will explain the better promises that covenant brings.

23.brief: There were many priests under the old order, because death prevented them from continuing in office. Each priest’s ministry came to an end, and another had to take his place.
23.explain: “prevented by death from continuing” The many priests of the former order show the limitation of that office. Death stopped one man’s ministry, and another took his place. No earlier priest could continue on behalf of God’s people indefinitely.

24.brief: Jesus continues forever, and so He has “an unchangeable priesthood.” Because He lives forever, His priesthood never passes to anyone else.
24.explain: “He continues forever” Jesus’ priesthood is permanent because Jesus Himself lives forever. The office never needs to pass to a successor, and His people have a Priest whose service never ends.

25.brief: Therefore Jesus is able “to save to the uttermost those who come to God through Him, since He always lives to make intercession for them.” His salvation is complete and lasting, because He never stops interceding for those who draw near to God through Him.
25.explain: “save to the uttermost” Jesus saves completely and forever those who draw near to God through Him. His continual intercession means He is always there to act on their behalf. Their assurance rests on this living Priest and the sufficient offering He made once for all.

26.brief: Such a High Priest fits our need: holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and exalted higher than the heavens. Jesus is the sinless and exalted priest that sinners require.
26.explain: “holy, harmless, undefiled” The High Priest who meets our need is holy, innocent of evil, and untouched by sin. His separation from sinners identifies His purity, and His exaltation above the heavens places Him in God’s presence for them.

27.brief: Unlike the other high priests, who had to offer sacrifices daily, first for their own sins and then for the people’s, Jesus had no sins of His own to atone for. He made His offering for the people “once for all when He offered up Himself,” and that single sacrifice is complete and never needs repeating.
27.explain: “once for all when He offered up Himself” The earlier priests needed repeated sacrifices for their sins and then for those of the people. Jesus had no sins of His own to atone for. He offered Himself for His people in a single sacrifice whose effect endures.

28.brief: The law appoints as high priests men who have weakness, “but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son who has been perfected forever.” God’s later oath establishes the Son, who has completed His saving calling, as High Priest forever.
28.explain: “the Son who has been perfected forever” The law appointed men subject to weakness. God’s later oath appoints the Son, who has reached the intended end of His saving calling and holds the office forever. His completed offering and continuing priesthood give the congregation its lasting confidence.
